references.app_or_product: Webtoon, Choices, Episode or a phone visual novel (choices between strip panels)
references.screen: A vertical comic reader with a decision placed between panels
references.what_it_shows: Not in Lazyweb. Webtoon appears only as discovery, library, schedule and pop-up screens, with no episode reader. No Choices, Episode or visual-novel app turned up in 14 screen searches and 2 flow searches. Every description below is Lazyweb's own text about the screen. I did not open the images, because this task allowed no browser and no downloads.
references.lesson_for_retake: Nobody shows how a strip should hand over to a decision, so nothing proves it. The join (the last panel ends on the asker's goal, then the full decision step) has to be drawn on the parts sheet and played by the owner. It cannot be copied from a shipped app.

references.screen: 'read a book' flow: book detail, reader cover, picture page with speech bubbles, end screen with Take Quiz or Read Again
references.what_it_shows: A 4-step flow. The reading page is a full illustration with speech-bubble text and almost no controls. The questions come after the story as their own step ('Take Quiz'), with an upgrade grid under the end screen.
references.lesson_for_retake: Reading and answering stay apart: the strip beats carry no controls, and each decision is its own full step screen (question at 104, dock at 748) between runs of the strip. Leave out the promo grid on the end screen.

references.what_it_shows: A full-page illustration with the dialogue in speech bubbles and no visible UI.
references.lesson_for_retake: Supports live-text bubbles over a text-free painting, with the header cut to '?' and Skip. Each strip beat should look like a page, not like a form.

references.screen: Lesson: character dialogue with a choice under it
references.what_it_shows: A cartoon character's line sits at the top. A multiple-choice selector sits below it, with a microphone button.
references.lesson_for_retake: The speaker's line goes up top and the choices go in the bottom band, which matches the Reach rule. Retake's choices are equal-size person cards, though, never lines to say: the player's own line is fixed (rule 38).

references.what_it_shows: A lesson told as a dark-mode chat between two drawn characters who ask and answer a simple question (pizza or pasta).
references.lesson_for_retake: Shows that a short drawn exchange can carry one question quickly. Retake tells this through panels and bubbles, not a chat log, because the owner ruled out the group chat.

references.screen: Speech-bubble question with Check disabled until a pick
references.what_it_shows: A word in a speech bubble, answer buttons below, and a 'Check' button that stays disabled until an answer is chosen.
references.lesson_for_retake: The same pick-then-confirm as Retake's, with the main button inert until a card is picked. After confirming, Retake must show no right-or-wrong panel.

references.screen: 'complete roleplay' flow: animated scene, completion, feedback review, results
references.what_it_shows: An animated story scene with a top progress bar, then a 'you did it' screen, a review of a corrected reply, and a result with stars, words used, a 'new record' badge and XP.
references.lesson_for_retake: Copy the outline: scene, short wrap-up, one Continue. Drop the stars, records, XP and 'corrected' review, because a Retake decision has no right answer and the result shows only plain counts.

references.what_it_shows: Narrative text with a 'tap to continue' prompt, plus two profile slots (Character and You) with swap icons.
references.lesson_for_retake: One tap per beat and nothing moves on by itself (rule 40). Leave out the 'You' profile and character swap: the player is never drawn and never picks an avatar.

references.what_it_shows: A dark, minimal screen: one line of story text, page dots showing where you are, and one main button.
references.lesson_for_retake: With 4 or 5 questions in about 2 minutes, a few dots over Next (as DESIGN.md already places them) tell the player how short today's strip is, at no cost to the word budget.

references.screen: Pick a person from four name cards
references.what_it_shows: A prompt with an emoji, a 2/12 counter, a grid of four name cards to pick 'the correct person' from, and score counters at the foot.
references.lesson_for_retake: Picking a person from a grid with a small question count is a familiar game shape for adults. Leave out the 'correct person' framing and the running score.

references.what_it_shows: A 'who' question about people, with large options (either partner, both, neither) and a progress count.
references.lesson_for_retake: 'Who should...' over people's cards reads as a normal everyday question. 'Both' and 'neither' would let the player dodge choosing between the equal two, and 20 questions is four times a daily level.

references.screen: Start screen: choose Easy, Medium or Hard
references.what_it_shows: Three large primary buttons (Easy, Medium, Hard) under a short tagline, with Back.
references.lesson_for_retake: The best-known version of the three-level choice. Retake's level switch can be three equal buttons or segments on today's cover over the one shared scene, each showing whether it is played. The tagline is not needed under the 20-word budget.

references.screen: Home: today's puzzle card with mode tabs and archives
references.what_it_shows: A greeting and date, a segmented control (mini, midi) plus an archives tab, and today's card with a play icon, duration, difficulty and one Play. A Pro upgrade sits beside them.
references.lesson_for_retake: Puts the level as a segment on today's card with a time hint ('about 2 min') and keeps the archive (Past puzzles) as its own tab, away from today. No Pro lock on a level.

references.what_it_shows: Five levels (Relaxed, Easy, Default, Tough, Very Hard), each with a description and progress counts, and a check on the current one.
references.lesson_for_retake: Progress shown as counts per level is a useful idea ('2 of 3 played today'). Five levels and a description each would break the word budget, so keep three short labels.

references.screen: Games hub with Packs and Archive
references.what_it_shows: A welcome line, a grid of today's puzzle tiles, and shortcuts to Packs and Archive.
references.lesson_for_retake: Today stays front and centre, and the archive is a shortcut. That matches Past puzzles opening only on a tap and counting toward All time only.

references.what_it_shows: Daily games as tappable cards in sections ('More sudokus', 'Weekend crosswords').
references.lesson_for_retake: For contrast: a hub of many puzzles. Retake's day is one scene with three levels, so its cover should not turn into a catalogue.

references.what_it_shows: Today's personalised set of games with one Start button, status counters and a premium banner.
references.lesson_for_retake: One Start for today's set suits a player who plays all three levels in a row. But each Retake level is the same for everyone, so nothing is 'personalised', and there is no banner.

references.screen: Streak start with a week row
references.what_it_shows: A large '1 day' streak count, a row of the week's days, a 'commit' button and Share.
references.lesson_for_retake: A seven-day row under the streak count is the standard way to show a week. Leave out the commit pressure, and leave out Share until sharing exists (M5).

references.screen: Daily question done: 1-day streak and week tracker
references.what_it_shows: A flame, '1 day streak', the week with today ticked, and a line asking you to come back for the next daily question.
references.lesson_for_retake: The done state says when the next one arrives, like Retake's decided 'Next puzzle in 3 h'. Use no flame and no congratulations, because 'well done' is banned.

references.what_it_shows: A modal that gives counts only: correct answers, incorrect answers and unsolved answers, with Close.
references.lesson_for_retake: The clearest plain-count result found: counts in buckets, no score. Retake has no 'correct', so its buckets count the player's own choices ('kept your rule in 3 of 4', '4 of 5 settled').

references.screen: Practice results: Got it and Needs review
references.what_it_shows: Two groups of cards with counts ('Got it', 'Needs review'), a circular percentage and the date.
references.lesson_for_retake: Two counted groups with small pictures work. Drop the percentage ring, which reads as a score, and the judging words.

references.what_it_shows: A checklist of what was studied, each item ticked, and one 'Review more' button.
references.lesson_for_retake: A result can simply list what was done: each decision as a job and a number, ticked, with no names and no grade (rule 46). Then one button, 'Back to today'.

references.what_it_shows: Played, win %, current streak, max streak and a guess distribution chart.
references.lesson_for_retake: 'Played', 'current streak' and 'longest streak' are plain counts and can stay. Win % and the distribution are scores and comparisons, which the result must not show.

references.what_it_shows: Puzzles solved, solve rate, current and longest streak, and a solve-time chart by weekday.
references.lesson_for_retake: 'Puzzles solved' and the streaks are fine. Solve rate and weekday time charts compare days and show change over time, and the research line rules both out.

references.screen: Statistics with lifetime totals and a schedule by day
references.what_it_shows: Lifetime totals (puzzles, words), highest rank, a This Week / Last Week toggle and a list by day.
references.lesson_for_retake: Lifetime totals as plain numbers fit 'All time'. Leave out ranks and the week-against-week toggle.

references.what_it_shows: A congratulation for finishing an Easy puzzle, the solve time, 'play another' and a promo for another game.
references.lesson_for_retake: One clear next action after a level (the next level, or 'Back to today'). Show no solve time (no clocks, rule 40) and no congratulation copy.

references.what_it_shows: Activity counts for each day of the week, a weekly goal with Edit, and an upgrade prompt.
references.lesson_for_retake: Plain counts by day suit the Week tab ('Tue: 3 levels'). Leave out goal-setting and the upgrade.

references.what_it_shows: A celebration with speaking accuracy, 'correct on first try' and sentences in a row.
references.lesson_for_retake: The opposite of what Retake needs: accuracy and first-try correctness imply right answers. Use none of it.

references.screen: Streak with rescues and a month calendar
references.what_it_shows: The current streak, the previous record, 'rescues' (streak freeze) marks with an info tip, a month calendar of activity, and Share.
references.lesson_for_retake: Draw the forgiven day as its own mark on the week itself, so a forgiven gap looks different from a break and from a played day. Leave out the record and Share.

references.what_it_shows: The day streak, a message about earning streak freezes, Personal and Friends tabs, a month calendar, and figures for days practised, freezes used and a progress rating.
references.lesson_for_retake: 'Freezes used' shown as a plain count beside the calendar is clear. Retake's one forgiven day a week is automatic (already decided), so there is nothing to earn or buy. Leave out the Friends tab (Board hidden until accounts) and the rating.

references.screen: Vacation status and streak save count
references.what_it_shows: A vacation-mode state with days left, an 'end vacation' control, and a count of streak saves with a 'how it works' link.
references.lesson_for_retake: Showing what is left as a count ('1 forgiven day this week') answers 'what happens if I miss?' without a sheet of rules. A vacation mode is more machinery than one forgiven day needs.

references.screen: Streak: days and weeks in a row
references.what_it_shows: The day streak and 'weeks in a row', a month calendar and a records section.
references.lesson_for_retake: Counting whole weeks is forgiving by nature and fits Retake's week of one world, ending in Sunday's look again. This is an idea for the owner, not a decided rule.

references.what_it_shows: A month calendar with ticked days, 'days this month' and 'week streak'.
references.lesson_for_retake: 'Days played this month' is a plain count that never shames a gap.

references.what_it_shows: Tells the user the streak is lost and gives calm guidance to get back on track with a short session.
references.lesson_for_retake: When a streak does break after the forgiven day, keep it calm: one plain line and today's levels, with no guilt and no 'oops' (both banned).

references.what_it_shows: A calendar grid of past daily puzzles with a month dropdown and arrows. You tap a day to open its puzzle.
references.lesson_for_retake: A good shape for Past puzzles. Retake's version must fetch a day only when it is opened, never count it toward the streak or the week, and keep back the other half of a hidden pair for 7 days.

references.what_it_shows: A calendar-style tracker where the streak is kept by meeting weekly targets, not daily ones.
references.lesson_for_retake: More evidence that streaks counted by the week are an accepted, gentler unit.

references.what_it_shows: Selling a way to recover missed days, with a discounted yearly price and a countdown timer.
references.lesson_for_retake: Avoid. A forgiven day must never be sold or put behind a timer.

references.what_it_shows: A streak calendar with points for each date, a reminder toggle and an 'awarded' pop-up.
references.lesson_for_retake: Avoid. Points for showing up turn the week into a reward chart.

patterns: Reading and answering are separate. Story pages carry speech bubbles and almost no controls, and questions come as their own screens at set points (Epic read-a-book, Duolingo roleplay). For Retake: runs of text-free panels with live bubbles, each ending on the asker's goal, then the standard decision step. The strip never holds the cards.
One tap per beat with a few page dots (character.ai, Tapotron). Nothing moves on by itself, and the dots over Next show the player that today's strip is short (4 or 5 questions, about 2 minutes).
Pick, then confirm, with the main button inert until a pick (Duolingo Check). This matches R-STEP-8 and the One Yellow Rule.
A small question count ('2 of 5') or dots on a people-picking question is familiar to adults from party quizzes (Peek, Couple Joy). It fits the 15-word budget.

Three levels as three equal buttons or segments on one screen (NYT Sudoku Easy, Medium, Hard; Crossword Chef's mode tabs). For Retake: on today's cover, over the one shared scene, each level showing to play or played, plus a time hint.

Past puzzles live in their own tab or archive calendar and open only on a tap (NYT Games Archive, the Connections archive grid, Crossword Chef archives). That keeps them away from today, the streak and the week.
The done state says when the next one comes (Couple Joy's 'come back for the next daily question'), the same as Retake's decided 'Next puzzle in 3 h'.

Results as counts in buckets or a ticked checklist, with no score (Guardian 'Check crossword': correct, incorrect, unsolved; Codecademy Go's checklist). In Retake the buckets count the player's own choices ('kept your rule in 3 of 4'), and the list names a job and a number, never a person.
Lifetime and streak figures as plain counts: played, current streak, longest streak, all-time totals (NYT Wordle and Spelling Bee stats, minus their scores).
The week as a seven-day row, today marked (Duolingo, Couple Joy). The Week tab can add plain counts per day (Babbel) or 'days played this month' (BoldVoice).

The forgiven day drawn on the calendar as its own mark, different from both played and missed (Drops rescues, Duolingo 'freezes used'), with what is left shown as a count (Alma's streak saves). Retake's version is automatic, one a week, with nothing to earn.
A calm line after a broken streak, then today's levels (Gentler). No guilt.

Streaks counted in whole weeks (Speak's 'weeks in a row', Codecademy Go's weekly targets) are an accepted, gentler unit. It suits a week of one world ending in Sunday's look again, but it is for the owner to decide, not a rule.

Evidence basis: every description comes from Lazyweb's own screen text. The images were not opened, because this task allowed no browser and no downloads. Check by eye on the Lazyweb page before copying any detail.
avoid: Stars, XP, 'new record', accuracy, 'correct on first try', win %, solve rate, guess distributions and ranks (Duolingo roleplay result, Falou, NYT stats). A Retake decision has no right answer, and the result shows only plain counts until the research line sets a score.

Comparisons: This Week against Last Week, weekday solve-time charts, level against level (NYT Crossword and Spelling Bee stats). The research draft says levels are never compared and there is no change over time.
Right-or-wrong feedback after confirming (Duolingo's Check panel), 'the correct person' framing (Peek), and judging bucket names like 'Needs review' (Capwords).
Solve times and countdown timers in or after a puzzle (NYT Sudoku completion, timed word games). Rule 40 allows no clocks.
Congratulation copy, flames, commit-to-your-streak prompts and Share buttons (Duolingo, Couple Joy, NYT Sudoku). 'Well done' is banned, and sharing waits for M5.

Selling or gamifying the missed day: paid streak repair behind a timer (Mimo), points for check-ins (Shein), freezes earned as rewards (Duolingo). Retake's one forgiven day a week is automatic and free.
Friends streaks, leaderboards and Friends tabs (Duolingo). The Board stays hidden until accounts exist.
Picking or showing a 'You' avatar or profile (character.ai, Smartdreams). The player is never drawn and has no gender.
Telling the story as a chat log (Duolingo dialogue chat, character.ai). The owner ruled out the group chat, so the daily is panels with bubbles.
Choice lists of lines for the player to say (Falou phrases, visual-novel menus). The player's lines are fixed and the same whatever is picked (rule 38). The only choice is the people on the cards.
'Both' and 'neither' options (Couple Joy). They let the player step around choosing between the equal two.
Taglines and a description under each level (NYT Sudoku tagline, Art of Fauna's five described levels). They break the 15 and 20 word budgets. Three short labels are enough.
'Personalised' daily plans (Elevate). Each Retake level is the same for everyone at that level.
Turning the cover into a catalogue of many puzzles (Guardian, Washington Post hubs). A Retake day is one scene with three levels.
Upgrade grids, Pro locks on a level and promo cards on end screens (Epic, Crossword Chef, NYT, Babbel).

Treating any shipped app as proof of how the strip should hand over to a decision. Lazyweb has no Webtoon reader and no Choices or Episode screens, so that join has to be drawn on the parts sheet and played by the owner.

proposals.name: One scene in three parts
proposals.one_line: Each day is one everyday scene told as a three-part comic strip: Easy is its start (8 pm), Medium its middle (9 pm), Hard its end (10 pm). Each part stands alone and plays in about 2 minutes, always in the same shape: the place, the asker at your door, a list of four jobs, two questions, a breather, two questions, then what came of it. The weekday's own character asks every question (Shobha Aunty every Monday, in whatever look that week has), and a second voice banters with her. A player who plays all three gets the whole evening with nothing repeated. Seven paintings a day.
proposals.how_a_level_plays:
The same 13 screens in every part, every day and every world. One button at the bottom always names the next step, and a tap anywhere on a story panel does the same. No swipes, no timers. Every beat is saved, so the cover reads Continue and the strip reopens at the same beat. Times are estimates for a player who has met the kinds before, given as Easy / Medium / Hard:
0 Cover: the day's painting, title, level switch (Easy, Medium, Hard) with each part's start time, Play. 4 / 3 / 3 s.
1 The place: the people-free lane painting with a time box ("8:05 pm. Lights out. The whole lane is outside.") and the part's 12 neighbours as small faces with names, all one size, shuffled. 4 / 3 / 3 s.
2 At your door: the asker and the second voice talk to each other and to you, then your fixed line. 5 s.
3 The list: four jobs with empty boxes ("Before nine: Office call, Candle money, One plug, Two lamps"), button "First job". The list then shrinks into the top bar as four boxes beside the story clock. 4 s.
4 Question 1: a sheet rises over the strip; you pick, then confirm. 16 / 18 / 26 s.
5 Stamp: the sheet folds into "Office call: settled" in the strip and box 1 fills; button "Next job". 2 s.
6 Question 2. 20 / 24 / 24 s.
7 Breather: the second voice's panel, two lines about the event, never about the cards. 4 s.
8 Question 3. 15 / 20 / 26 s.
9 Stamp. 2 s.
10 Question 4. 18 / 17 / 20 s.
11 What came of it: the outcome painting reprints as the world's cover (Lugdi's pulp reprint, at most 1.2 s, a tap skips it) and the stamp lands by band ("All set: 9:00 / 9:15 / 9:40"). 5 s.
12 Reaction: the asker's line, which changes by band only and is warm in every band; your fixed reply; button "See today". 4 s.
13 Result: plain counts, an offer of the next part, Back to today. 5 s.
Totals: Easy 1:48, Medium 1:56, Hard 2:13, so about 6 minutes for all three, inside the owner's 5 to 7. About 20 taps a part. First-time extras: a moving hand the first time each kind is met (about 4 s each) and name labels the first time the cast is met, so a launch-day Easy for someone who skipped the First take runs about 1:56. If the playtest median for a part goes past 2:15, or a day past 7 minutes, cut the breather first, then merge the place and the door into one beat. A question is never cut.
proposals.panels_per_day:
Seven paintings a day: 42 a week, 84 for the two weeks before launch.
1) L, the place, people-free, wide 2:1 with a portrait crop for phones. It is shared by all three levels: the cover, the first beat of every part (each with its own time box and faces), and the backdrop behind all 12 questions. It is people-free so no painted face sits behind the cards (rule 32).
2) to 4) One people panel per level (E-W, M-W, H-W), wide 2:1. The left crop is that part's door beat and the right crop is its breather; a laptop shows the whole painting.
5) to 7) One outcome painting per level (E-O, M-O, H-O). H-O is L's view with every light on.
Not paintings: the job list and stamps (app parts in the world's paperwork), the cast's face chips (one present-day portrait each, painted once), and card portraits (from the portrait library).
Wide 2:1 panels are still an owner choice in the bubble spec. Without them the day needs ten paintings. The cheaper fallback, three versions of one moment, needs four a day but makes the second and third play repeat the strip.
In the queue, the First take's 46 panels took 2.5 to 4 hours, so a week of dailies is about one night plus repaints after the text check, run only through heavyq on the owner's Mac.
proposals.questions:
Where they sit: four questions, always at the same four places: two right after the list, a breather panel, two more. The rhythm "two, a breather, two" never changes, so a regular player knows how far along they are without reading. It is four, not five, because with 4 or 5 cards each, five questions would push a part past 2:30 and the day past 7 minutes.
Who asks: one asker a day for all three parts, and the same asker on that weekday every week (Shobha Aunty every Monday, in that week's look). Six askers, 3 women and 3 men, each on a model sheet. Because a twin's second half comes next week on the same weekday, both halves are asked by the same person (rule 37). Hari Chacha is the one comic voice: he never asks and never sits on a card. The question sits in the asker's balloon with her face chip at the fixed question place (104 px). On a hard-topic question it goes in the plain question box, never in a bubble. The balloon gives the goal of the moment plus the ask in 10 words or fewer ("Shop shuts at 8:30. Which two collect the candle money?"), never the number the two tie on.
How the cards appear: tapping "First job" or "Next job" raises a full-screen sheet over the strip (420 ms; at once under reduced motion) in the First take's fixed skeleton: top bar (Back, the four job boxes and the story clock, "?"), the asker's balloon, the key ("Answered · Late"), the cards, the dock. All cards arrive together in a fresh shuffled order. A four-card pick one is a 2 x 2 grid of tiles; a five-card team, a rank or checks are rows. Each card has a portrait, name, two numbers with icons and one note under the world's margin rule; a judging note carries its speaker's face chip.
How the player answers: as today. Tap a card (pick yellow); the button wakes and names the consequence ("Sunita makes the call", "Send Deepak and Kavya"); tap it. The commit holds 260 ms, then the sheet folds into the job's stamp in the strip ("Office call: settled", the job word only, never a name or face) and that job's box fills in the top bar. Back before the commit returns to the strip with nothing answered. A settled job reopens read-only with a padlock. On resume, a question keeps its first card order. Until the fourth question every reaction is the same, whoever was picked.
proposals.levels:
The three levels are three parts of one evening in story time: Easy 8 to 9 pm ("Before nine"), Medium 9 to 10 ("Before ten"), Hard 10 to 11 ("Before eleven"). Each has its own time box, people panel, list of four jobs and outcome. Each stands alone: a Medium-only player starts with one line that says where things are ("9:00 pm. Still dark. The motor's off too."). No level depends on another level's answers or band.
What changes (owner answer 11, rule 55):
- Easy: one leaning note on one of the two; clear numbers (in a pick one the two are best on both numbers); kinds pick one and pick a team; 4 or 5 cards; a second tie of two women or two men in 2 of 4 questions; about 1:48.
- Medium: a second leaning note on a card outside the two, or a reason that matters on one of the two (that job's outcome is fixed); one card above the two on each number in rank and checks; kinds pick one, rank and checks; 4 cards; about 1:56.
- Hard: the two in the middle of the numbers, each with a leaning note (the notes change sides in the twin), or a returning pair that differs only in something that is not gender; one card leads on one number but misses the bar on the other (the day's trap); kinds rank and pick a team; 4 or 5 cards; about 2:13.
Every level keeps rule 20's decoy and one heavy-sounding fact on a decoy, and the day uses at least three kinds.
The second and third time: the player never sees the same strip again. They see the next part of the evening: the same lane painting with a new time box (one tap), then a new people panel, a new list, four new questions and a new outcome, and Hard ends on the lights coming back. What carries over is only what helps: the key is the same all day (short form after the first part), the cast is already known (no labels), and a kind already met gets no moving hand. So the story costs about 20 seconds in the second and third parts. Playing out of order is fine, because the level switch shows each part's start time. People: the day has one lane of 18 neighbours drawn from a standing pool of about 60 faces. Each part shows 12 of them. Each person keeps the same numbers all evening. Nobody sits in an equal pair at more than one level that day.
proposals.equal_two:
1) Every question has an equal two, so no question looks special, and every part has a second tie between two women or two men.
2) The strip never touches the cards. Card people are never painted. They appear only as cards and once as the part's row of small faces, all one size and shuffled. No bubble, caption, stamp, breather line or your line names anyone on the cards, points at them, describes them or uses their note words; the checker refuses any that do. The asker's balloon gives only the goal of the moment, never the number the two tie on.
3) The nudge lives only in a card note, said by a named voice with a face chip; both a woman's voice (Shobha) and a man's (Hari) speak in every part. Another card always has a decoy note of the same kind. In each question and each language, notes are within 2 words of each other. The two's notes are the same length and never share an opening word or frame, and the longest note falls on the two in a quarter to a half of questions (the sample: 2 of 4).
4) Your lines are fixed and never change with the pick or state a rule for choosing. Stamps name the job only. No reaction changes until after the fourth question.
5) Outcomes come from numbers only. Each bar sits at or below the two's numbers, so either of the two gives the same outcome, and "always the woman" ends the same as "always the man". Cards that miss a bar are as often men as women (the sample: 4 and 4). Outcome lines name the event, never a person, and a reason that matters has a fixed outcome.
6) Across levels and weeks: nobody is in a pair at more than one level that day. Each twin's second half comes next week, at the same weekday, level, question place and asker, in the next world's look, with a new place, task and people and the nudge on the other side. Each part opens two twins and closes two. In launch week the other two questions carry a pair that is never read.
7) The result never lists picks: no names, no faces, no row of who got what, only counts.
8) Inside a part, pair members match on earlier card appearances, and nobody who was weakest earlier sits in a later pair (rule 17). The sample deck passes this.
Known gap: a player who knows the rules can still spot the one woman-and-man tie, because the second tie is always same-gender.
proposals.words:
What counts: speech, your lines, narration, sound words, labels, sign words and buttons. What does not: names, kinship names used as names, numbers and times. Budgets: 15 on a puzzle screen (question 10 or fewer, with notes held by the note rule) and 20 elsewhere; a spoken line 10 or fewer, narration 12 or fewer. Speech is counted, which is stricter than the 21 Oct rule while question 14 is open. English counts from check_sample.py, against the budget:
Cover 11/20.
Place beat 8/20.
Door beat 20/20 the first time the cast is met (labels "Shobha Aunty, keeps the lane's keys" and "Hari Chacha, next door"), then 14/20 on later Mondays.
List 12/20.

risks: Timing is estimated, not measured: four questions of four or five cards may run past 2 minutes for slower readers, the 61-year-old and Hindi readers, and the day past 7 minutes. First cut: the breather beat; second: merge the place and the door beats.

Painting load: 7 paintings a day, 42 a week and 84 before launch, plus repaints after the text check, all on the owner's 24 GB Mac through heavyq only. Keeping Shobha's face the same across five looks is hard for FLUX. Fallback: three versions of one moment (4 paintings a day), at the cost of repeats on the second and third play.

Three parts can read as an order: Medium-only players always start mid-evening, some players may feel they must play Easy first, and someone who plays Hard first knows the lights come back before playing Easy.

The weekday asker crosses worlds (Shobha every Monday in every look). That goes beyond the owner's 23 Oct 'one person, one world', which was said of the First take household, so it needs the owner's yes. The same asker every Monday may also come to feel like 'the easy one'.

Twin bookkeeping with four questions: each part opens two twins and closes two. In launch week two questions a part carry a pair that is never read, and Sunday's 'What was different?' has no finished twin until week 2. The research line has to agree.

A player who knows the rules can still find the pair: the equal two are the only woman-and-man tie, and the second tie is always two women or two men. In the sample, the pair's members also first appear on cards in their own question in three of four questions.
One key all day (Answered, Late) can feel samey across twelve questions and makes writers strain to tie every job to it.
Faces recur across parts and days, and liking a face leaks into picks (the shaadi demo's lesson). Cap it: a face on at most two days a week and in at most one pair a week, from a pool of about 60.
Word budgets are tight: the first-meeting door beat is exactly 20, Hindi questions sit near the 10-word cap, and Hindi screen totals were not counted here.

The scene and the look: a power cut may fail the twice-a-week everyday test for the metro player (a prediction only), and Lugdi's torchlit pulp drama can tip into menace on the easiest day of the week.
'4 of 4 on time' on the result may read as a score. The tomorrow teaser on the done cover may read as a push and could hint at a hard-topic day's setting.
Five-card questions run past a 360 x 640 phone in Hindi behind the 'more' cue (ground-rules question 16 is open).
Wide 2:1 paintings (one painting, two crops) are an owner choice not yet made in the bubble spec; without them the day needs ten paintings.
Jobs show only in plain notes, so some cards never show a job. Showing a job on every card would mean counting it under the note rule, not the 15-word screen budget.

The Saal Bhar checkers and deck solver lived in a scratchpad that a reboot wipes. A whole-day solver (18 neighbours, fixed numbers, three levels) is new work, and it is a prerequisite for writing two weeks.

proposals.name: The six-painting day
proposals.one_line: Each day is one everyday scene painted as six text-free pictures. All three levels share the place picture, the asker's panel and the world's big moment, and each level adds one painted turn of its own. A level reads as a four-beat comic strip with four questions in about two minutes, and the launch fortnight costs 72 painting jobs plus 18 character references (about 12 hours of queue, four nights).
proposals.how_a_level_plays:
A tap brings the next beat into the scrolling strip. Nothing moves by itself, scrolling up rereads, and Back works. A question opens as the app's existing step screen over the day picture. Its confirm tap folds it into a settled stub in the strip (a tick, the job word and a lock, with no name or face) and brings the next beat.

Easy, played first today (about 1:50):
- Cover, with the day title and the level's problem; Play: 4 s (0:04).
- B1 opening, a crop of the wide day picture with narration and the regular speaking from off the panel; Next: 5 s (0:09).
- B2, the regular face-on asking for help, plus the player's fixed reply; Next: 6 s (0:15).
- Q1, pick one from 4: 18 s (0:33).
- Q2, pick one from 4: 20 s (0:53).
- B3, the level's turn; Next: 6 s (0:59).
- Q3, pick a team of 2 from 5: 22 s (1:21).
- Q4, pick one from 4: 18 s (1:39).
- B4 outcome, the world's big moment over the day picture with the level's stamp and the regular's fixed line for the band: 6 s (1:45).
- Result, plain counts; Back to today: 5 s (1:50).

Medium, played second (about 1:55): cover 4, B2 6 (B1 is skipped), Q1 pick one 18, Q2 pick one with a reason that matters 22, B3 6, Q3 spend 2 checks among 5 22, Q4 rank 4 26, B4 6, result 5.

Hard, played third (about 2:07): cover 4, B2 6, Q1 pick one from 5 22, Q2 team of 3 from 5 28, B3 6, Q3 rank 5 30, Q4 pick one 20, B4 6, result 5.

All three come to about 5:52. A level played first today adds B1's 5 s. In Hindi a day runs about 6:30. The moving hand the first time a kind appears adds about 5 s, once.
proposals.panels_per_day:
Six painting jobs a day, about 40 minutes of queue.

Shared by all three levels:
- Jobs 1 and 2, the day picture, people-free, in portrait and in wide, at 6 tries each because it is the most-seen picture. It serves:
  - all three covers;
  - B1, as the left 4:3 crop of the wide;
  - the background of all 12 questions (portrait on phones, wide on laptops);
  - every level's B4 outcome, dressed in the world's big moment (Lugdi: the cover reprints) with the level's stamp in live text.
- Job 3, B2: the day's regular face-on, looking out at the player. The same painting is used at all three levels with new bubbles. It is painted with the edit model from the regular's reference for the week's look, with job 2 as the place reference.

Own per level:
- Jobs 4 to 6, one B3 turn each: a people-free close-up of an object, or the regular from behind, painted with job 2 as the place reference.

No painted lead-ins and no painted "happened" beats. Written the First take's way, the same day would need about 27 jobs.

Launch fortnight:
- 72 day jobs (about 8 h).
- 18 one-off references for the six regulars: one master each, then Lugdi and Station (about 1.5 h).
- Repaints, budgeting a third of jobs once (about 2.5 h).
- In all, about 12 h: three nights plus one for repaints.

Sundays need no new painting: the library's Sunday drawings sit over the week's pictures.

Ongoing: 36 jobs a week, one night. Each new world also needs 6 references once.

Human time on the art is about 25 minutes a day: six seed picks, one face close-up, and 7 bubble placements in two anchor sets.

On a lean day, one B3 can be shared by all three levels, for 4 jobs.
proposals.questions:
There are four questions per level, two each side of the turn: B2, Q1, Q2, B3, Q3, Q4, B4. Four rather than five, because five pushes Hard past 2:30. A fifth is allowed only if timing shows a level under 1:45.

Who asks: the day's regular asks every question at every level. The question sits in their bubble at the fixed question place (top at 104 px) with their present-day face chip; today's Step.speaker and speakerFace already do this. On a hard-topic question it sits in the plain question box, with no bubble.

How the cards appear: Next on the beat before a question slides the strip up, and the step screen fills the phone in the Fixed Skeleton:
- the top bar, with the day plate as its title;
- the regular's bubble with the question;
- the stat key, from a standing library of number sets with icons;
- 4 or 5 card people from the week's face pool, in a fresh shuffle;
- one button in the dock at 748 px.

How the player answers, as in the First take: pick one is a tap then confirm; team and checks are taps then the button; rank is moving rows. A revisited question is read-only with its lock. The confirm folds the step into a settled stub with the job word only.

Two kinds of question (new; this changes rule 13 for the dailies and waits for the owner's yes):
- A pair question carries the equal two and is one half of a twin.
- An open question has no woman-and-man tie anywhere. It has either two women or two men tied (at the top, or for a seat), or one clear best who carries a remark, which is the daily's trap.

From week 2, each strip holds two pair questions (one closing last week's twin, one opening a new one) and two open questions. In launch week the closing slot holds an open question.

Slots: the writer picks which two of the four slots carry pairs. A twin's second half sits in the same slot, at the same level, on the same weekday next week (rule 58), asked by the same regular. That makes the same asker, shape and lead-in hold by construction:
- slot 1 always follows B2;
- slot 3 always follows B3;
- slots 2 and 4 follow a settled stub.

A script checks that each slot carries a pair 2 to 4 times a week per level, never the same two slots three days running.

Kinds:
- Easy uses pick one and team.
- Medium adds checks and rank.
- Hard pair questions use rank, team, batting order or split.
- The launch fortnight uses only the kinds the app already has.
proposals.levels:
The same at all three levels: the day picture, the regular, the B2 painting, the evening and the outcome's frame.

Each level's own: a problem (named on its cover in live text), a B3 turn painting, a circle of 5 or 6 card people (nobody sits in an equal pair at more than one level that day), a number set, a target and a stamp.

The pair question changes by level (owner's answer 11, rule 55):
- Easy has one loaded-word nudge in a named voice on one of the two. The numbers are clear, with the two jointly best on both. There is a second tie between two women or two men, and a decoy remark of the nudge's kind.
- Medium adds either a reason that truly matters on one of the two (a "matters" twin) or a second leaning note on a card outside the two.
- Hard is a muddle. The two sit below the top (tied for the last seat in a team or rank), and/or the nudge is two leaning notes, one on each, which change sides in the twin.

The open questions change by level:
- Easy has one remark on a tied card.
- Medium has a practical fact that sounds as if it matters on a decoy, and one heavy-sounding decoy fact.
- Hard has two remarks and 5 cards.

Cards: 4 at Easy, 4 or 5 at Medium, 5 at Hard.

A player who plays all three sees no repeated text:
- The cover's level switch ticks the levels played, and the next level's cover names its own problem ("The ice run").
- The strip opens at B2. B1 is skipped, and Back rereads it.
- B2 is the same painting of the regular with a new problem in the bubble, read as the next thing to land on them that evening (a repeated-panel device).
- B3 is a painting they have not seen, and the cards carry new people.
- B4 is the same frame with this level's stamp.

So each later level shows one new painting and two familiar ones with new words.
proposals.equal_two:
Every rule below is a refusal in the day checker unless marked by eye.

1. Two casts.
   - The six regulars talk, ask and sign judging notes, and are never on a card.
   - Card people are never painted and speak no line. They appear only as their card portraits.
   - The player is never painted: people look out at them, and nothing is held from the player's side.
2. No bubble, narration, sign or player line names, points at, describes or uses the note words of anyone on the cards to come (rule 36, spec 7.2). The nudge lives only in card notes. Every judging note carries its speaker's face chip, and each level's judging notes come from at least two regulars, a woman and a man.
3. Stakes never mention women, men or roles tied to gender (the spec's word list, in both languages).
4. Reactions are the same whoever is picked.
   - The settled stub carries the job word only.
   - The outcome comes from the numbers only: the pair's numbers clear each bar, so swapping them changes nothing.
   - The regular's B4 line is fixed per band.
5. Every question carries a tie or a trap, so a tie is not a tell. Open questions never hold a woman-and-man tie, so only the pair does.
6. The notes give nothing away.
   - Notes run within 2 words of each other in each language, and the pair's are the same length.
   - The longest note falls on the pair in a quarter to a half of the week's pair questions.
   - The pair's notes share no opening word or sentence frame.
7. Twins are a week apart, in the next world's look, with new people, a new task and freshly worded nudges. Only the slot, the asker and the kind carry over, and those carry over for every question anyway.
8. The day picture and every B3 have no people, and B2 shows only the regular. Nothing in a picture is lit, held or pointed towards any card (by eye).

The strip itself sets only the scene and the goal ("Counter needs hands till 9"), never a skill that decides the pick or anything about a person.
proposals.words:
Counted: speech, the player's lines, narration, sound words, sign words, buttons and settled stubs. Not counted: names, kin names, numbers and times. Speech is counted, the stricter reading, so the page passes whichever way the owner answers question 14. Each language is counted on its own.

Budgets, with the sample's Easy level in English / Hindi:
- Cover: at most 20; day title at most 5, level problem at most 3. Sample 11 / 9.
- B1: at most 20, in at most 3 pieces; narration at most 12, a spoken line at most 10. Sample 13 / 11.
- B2: at most 20; the goal at most 10, the player's fixed line at most 5. Sample 12 / 14.
- Q1: at most 15, the question at most 10 (aim for 7, so the 4-word stat key and a 2 to 4 word button fit). Sample 12 / 14.
- Q2: at most 15. Sample 12 / 14.
- B3: at most 20; a sound word, one line and the stubs above. Sample 15 / 16.
- Q3: at most 15. Sample 14 / 14.
- Q4: at most 15. Sample 13 / 13.
- B4: at most 20; stamp at most 4, reaction at most 10. Sample 11 / 11.
- Result: at most 20. Sample 10 / 8.

Medium B2 is 14 / 15, and Hard B2 is 14 / 13.

Card notes sit outside the count, held by the note-length rule: aim for 4 to 6 words.

The strip story comes to about 130 counted words a day across all three levels.
proposals.sample:
TUESDAY, LUGDI WEEK (launch week, day 2): "Lights out at the store" | "दुकान की बत्ती गुल"

Scene: the corner general store in a narrow residential lane, 7:40 pm, a power cut. No festival and no city named. Life area: work; the family shop is one of rule 1's own examples of a narrower daily.

Regular: Manoj, 47, who runs the store, Tuesday's asker every week. Card people are lane neighbours with jobs most people can do, and judging notes carry the face chips of Asha (w, Monday's regular) and Joseph (m, Thursday's).

Number sets:
- Set A, "Counter evenings · Wrong sums" | "काउंटर की शामें · ग़लत हिसाब".
- Set B, "Errands · Times late" | "फेरे · देर से".

Each level opens one twin, in slot 2. Slot 4 is an open question in launch week.

PAINTINGS. Each prompt ends with Lugdi's style line and the text-free, unsigned ending, and uses role words, never names. The power cut keeps the shelves in deep shadow, so packets need no labels.

1 and 2. Day picture, portrait and wide, 6 tries each:
- The front of a small corner general store in a narrow lane at night, during a power cut, with the steel shutter half raised.
- A square white emergency lamp on a glass-topped counter throws hard white light. The shelves behind fall into deep violet shadow, showing only the shapes of plain tins and packets.
- Sacks of rice and dal with rolled-down tops stand at the step. Shut doors, a parked scooter and a dead streetlamp line the dark lane.
- No people. A plain night sky fills the top third.
- The wide version puts the store in the left third, with the dark lane carrying on to the right.

3. B2, edit model with the shopkeeper's Lugdi reference and the wide day picture as the place:
- The shopkeeper, 47, stands behind the counter in the left third, face-on. Medium-brown skin, a broad face, hair greying at the temples, a thick black moustache, rectangular steel spectacles, a mustard half-sleeve shirt under a grey sleeveless sweater, brass keys on a red cord.
- He holds the lamp up at shoulder height and looks straight out at the viewer, mouth open mid-word, his head a third of the way down.

risks: Lettered places (shop packets, crates, boards) draw stray letters. Dark scenes help, but shop and office days may need half their jobs repainted; prefer scenes with few lettered surfaces.

The regular's face can drift in B2, or the painter can add a bindi or lighten a woman regular's skin. Only one face panel a day is exposed, it is checked against the chip, and there is a from-behind fallback; a regular who keeps failing needs more reference views or a one-person LoRA test through heavyq.

The same four-beat shape every day may read as a template, which is the cheapness to avoid. Vary B3's camera and subject, the slots of the pairs and the regulars' small threads. The upgrade is a B2 for each level, for 8 jobs a day.

The story per level is thin: about 45 counted words around four questions. Depth has to come from the regulars recurring week after week, and threads that run across days wait on the owner's question 11.

Open questions without an equal two change rule 13 and need the owner's yes and the research line's view. Without them, a day needs 12 pair questions, twice the twin bookkeeping, and a tie becomes a tell.
Regulars asking in every world's look changes the owner's 23 Oct one-world call for the daily askers. The alternative means 30 character sheets, and twins asked by different people.
Launch week closes no twin, so the first Sunday has no side-by-side for 'What was different?', and no finished-twin count shows until week 2.
Writing, not painting, is the bottleneck: 72 questions and about 300 notes a week in two scripts, plus the weekly five-reader Hindi read.
Hard rank and team questions with 5 cards, in Hindi, may run past 2 min 30 s. Time the five newcomers before freezing week 1, and drop Hard to 4 cards if needed.
Hard-topic twins return on the same weekday, so two weeks running share a hard day. Move the hard weekday for each new pair of weeks.
The painting queue is shared with other sessions on a 24 GB Mac (heavyq only, never beside browsers), so the fortnight's four nights can slip.
The same day picture behind all 12 questions can make the decision screens feel static. The cards carry the change, and the wide stage can shift its focus crop by question.
Edit-model painting with the day picture as the place reference is untested; try it on the sample day before committing.

proposals.name: The chorus strip
proposals.one_line: Each level is a two-minute comic strip of one everyday scene. Two neighbours who comment on everybody are met before any card. Their signed remarks then fall evenly on women and men, on the equal two and on the others, so the nudge is just one voice in a chorus the player already knows. The strip itself only ever talks about the moment, never about the people on the cards.

proposals.questions:
- **Counts.** Easy has 5 questions with 4 cards each; Medium and Hard have 4 questions with 5 cards each.
- **Question roles.** Every level has exactly two measured questions (a new twin's first half and a returning second half), one trap (a near miss), and the rest steady (the numbers decide). In launch week the return slot holds a steady question.
- **Positions.** Each weekday and level has its own fixed pair of measured positions, so both halves of a twin sit at the same place. The sample Tuesday uses Easy 2 and 4, Medium 2 and 3, Hard 2 and 4.
- **Who asks.** One asker for the whole day at all three levels: the person running the scene (Sarla, the lane committee's head). Never a chorus voice, never a card person, never comic. Across a week the askers are 3 women and 3 men. Because a twin's halves are a week apart in a different scene, the two askers share gender, role kind and bubble shape, with the question's words within 2.
- **Where the question sits.** Each question follows one strip beat whose last bubble gives only the goal of the moment ("Lineman's tea, the diesel. All from this box."). Then the existing decision screen takes over: the question appears in the asker's bubble with her face chip at the fixed question place. On a hard-topic question it goes in the plain question box instead.
- **How the cards appear.** All at once, freshly shuffled on every load, over a people-free painting, with the key row. Easy uses tiles or rows; Medium and Hard use 5 rows. The first time a player meets a kind, a ghost hand demonstrates on blank cards, so it never moves towards a real person.
- **How the player answers.** By tapping (pick, team, rank, spend checks), then the yellow confirm button. The next beat shows a plate naming only the job ("Cash box: settled"), the same for every pick.
- **The outcome** comes only after the last question and only from the numbers. A placement counts unless someone left out was clearly ahead, so swapping the equal two never changes anything.
proposals.levels:
- **Easy.** 5 quick questions, 4 cards each. Kinds: pick one, team, rank. Numbers are clear.
  - Measured: the equal two are clearly best, with one remark (the nudge) on one of them. A decoy carries a remark of the same kind, and a second tie between two women or two men sits below.
  - Trap: a woman and a man one apart, with a remark pulling towards the weaker one.
- **Medium.** 4 questions, 5 rows each; spend checks join on the sample Tuesday. The cut falls inside a same-sex tie, so a tie between two women or two men fights over the last place.
  - Measured, alternating by weekday: either a "matters" twin (a reason that truly decides, such as the only driving licence, sits on one of the two) or a plain twin with a second leaning remark of a different kind on a decoy.
  - Trap: the mirrored near miss.
- **Hard.** 4 questions, 5 rows; numbers trade off against each other.
  - Measured: the two are tied in the middle with the cut between them. Each carries a remark of the same weight, and the remarks swap sides in the twin. A heavy-sounding fact sits on a decoy with an unmarked name.
  - Trap: the same-side tie, two women (or two men) tied and differing only by a remark. It has the same shape as a measured question with no gender in it, and shows how far a remark sways at all.
- **Across all three.** Each level has its own six people; nobody is on cards at two levels in a day, and no level mentions another level's events.
- **Playing a second or third level.** The day opener (the lane panel and the chorus panel) folds into a thin band showing a strip of the lane painting and the day's title; a tap unfolds it. The strip starts at that level's handover: the asker in new light, a new six on the circle beat, new moments, and a chorus beat with new lines. No panel is seen twice with the same words in a day.
proposals.equal_two:
The honest limit: the equal two match exactly on the numbers shown, so a player who scans every card can always find them. The design makes finding them useless rather than impossible. The only steady way through is to treat the same remark the same whoever carries it, which is the habit the trainer builds.

How the strip helps hide them:
1. **The chorus is met first.** The two commenters are introduced before any card, talking only about the day. Their faces then sign remarks on the cards. Kishore grumbles at everyone and Nusrat fusses fondly over everyone, so a remark's tone attaches to the speaker, not to the person it is about.
2. **Everyone is introduced equally.** The circle beat shows all six as identical, shuffled chips with names only.
3. **No bubble points at a card.** No bubble names, describes, or uses a content word from the note of anyone on a later card in that level. The check runs against every earlier bubble, not just the lead-in.
4. **Lead-ins look the same before every question,** whatever its role, and the chorus speaks before measured and steady questions equally often.
5. **Nothing reacts to a pick** until the outcome. Settled plates name only the job.

On the cards:
6. **Ties are everywhere.** In the sample's trust set, two women, two men and the equal two are all tied. At least 3 of Easy's 5 questions show an exact tie, and every measured question shows a second tie.
7. **Same-sex ties copy the measured shape.** In some steady questions two tied women or two tied men fight over the last place.
8. **The lone-gender rule.** At Easy, 4 cards plus a second tie forces a three-and-one split with the lone person in the pair. To offset this, steady questions also use three-and-one splits where the lone person is in no tie. In the sample the lone person is in the pair once out of four such questions.
9. **Notes are symmetric.** At Easy, the pair carries one remark and one plain fact, and so do the decoys. All notes are within 2 words of each other, and the pair's notes are equal in length. The nudge is never the only remark on the screen and never the longest note.
10. **Remarks balance.** In the sample, each voice makes 2 remarks about women and 2 about men, and women and men each get 2 kind and 2 unkind remarks.
11. **Histories match.** The pair have matched histories, with plain notes and neither ever the weakest card.
12. **Names.** Both members of a pair have community-marked names, or neither does.

Against "spot the sexist":
- **The nudge is an everyday remark** ("moody", "fussy", "spoilt"), never a claim about women or men.
- **The day's most stereotyped remark sits where the numbers already decide.** "Bossy" is on a woman who is clearly top for the keys.
- **Traps cut both ways.** They punish following remarks in either direction, alternating which sex gains from the pull.
- **Twins are mirrored.** Half the first nudges land on the man, and half the nudges are kind remarks.
- **"Matters" questions** break the rule "ignore every note when a woman and a man tie".
- **Hard's same-side tie** measures plain note-following separately from any lean.

Twins return next week on the same weekday, at the same level and position, with the same kind of question and the same kind of nudge on the other sex. A ledger refuses any other difference.

No daily result ever shows a pair count. A line like "treated 1 of 1 matching pairs alike" would send the player scrolling back to hunt for the pair, so finished-twin counts go on Sunday's week page instead.
